metadata.title: The World Is Falling - Extending Walker Jumpman
metadata.note: Walker-mode Godot walkthrough. B00 is a labelled reconstruction, never a transcript. All gameplay is native 3840x2160 captured from the running game; see CAPTURE.md. Claims are indexed in FACTCHECK.md.

beats.label: The ask
beats.narration_text: Please use Walker to convert my game design document into a playable Godot project. The premise: a world where gravity has failed and debris falls upward. The player finds an object that lets them fall upward too. And one rule underneath all of it - the world shows you what you expect, not what is actually there. Some floors exist but are never drawn. Some are drawn but are not there. The player checks by turning gravity upside down.
beats.reconstruction_label: Illustrative reconstruction of the design ask - not a historical transcript.

beats.label: What was built
beats.narration_text: This is walker-jumpman, the course starter by Nik Bear Brown - one short level, a few gaps, a spike, a finish flag, and a character drawn as four stacked rectangles. What you are about to see is that project extended by Narasimha Reddy Valam into something with an idea at the centre of it. The revision on screen throughout is commit c898a4b. The character is the Runner. The level is five times longer. And the mechanic is not a jump - it is a question the player has to keep asking about everything they can see.

artifactLines: STUDENT   Narasimha Reddy Valam
REVISION  c898a4b - the build shown throughout this film
STARTER   nikbearbrown/walker-jumpman @ 9387542
CHARACTER the Runner - trail length is horizontal speed
LEVEL     960 -> 4980 px; finish moved into a tower shaft
SCOPE     one chapter built; four designed and NOT built

qc.sparse_reason: A reference card read aloud, not a busy graphic. Six short lines on a dark plate is the point - the viewer is meant to read them while Liam speaks, and filling the safe area with decoration would make them harder to read, not easier.

beats.label: The world falls up
beats.narration_text: It tells you something is wrong and trusts you to notice. Rubble falls upward. And the trail behind the Runner is its own speed, so the character reports its state before the level has to.

qc.contrast_reason:
Gameplay plate, not a card, and two heuristics mis-fire on it.
full_bleed: the game renders edge to edge at 3840x2160. The world IS the frame, so crossing title-safe is the composition rather than overflow, and the HUD stays inside its own reserved bands.
contrast_regions: the whole-frame average is low because the upright palette is deliberately pale - light is the comfortable lie and dark is the truth, which is this chapter's mechanic rather than a rendering fault. The essential text is the PERSISTENT HUD, measured where hud.gd draws it: title, chapter and log count, controls row, and deaths/timer. Each must pass on its own.
The feather readout is deliberately NOT declared. It only exists after the player picks the feather up, so before that the region is legitimately empty - an earlier revision declared it and the gate correctly reported nine empty-region defects. Declaring a conditional element as persistent text would have been a false claim about the frame.

beats.narration_text: Gravity inverts. The trail goes cyan and the world goes black. Not a filter - in this chapter light is the comfortable lie and dark is what is actually there.

beats.narration_text: The idea at full strength. No floor is drawn here. Everything says walking forward is a fall. It is not. Invert, and the floor renders under your feet - it was always there.

beats.label: Signs that lie
beats.narration_text: And it lies in both directions, each with a rule behind it. A drawn platform holding nothing. A locked door you walk through. Spikes that cannot hurt you - and under a sign reading safe, spikes never drawn at all.

beats.label: Why a floor can be invisible
beats.narration_text: And here is the part worth stealing. None of that needed a new system. The starter already walked its level data twice - once to build a collider for every solid, once to paint them. Two loops that were always separate. Hidden geometry joins only the first, so it collides without ever being drawn. Phantom geometry joins neither, so it is drawn and holds nothing. No new node types, no physics change, not one collision check removed. The entire mechanic is the gap between two loops that were already there.

props.artifactTitle: Why a floor can be invisible
artifactLines: The starter already walked its level data twice:
_ready()  builds a collider for every solid
_draw()   paints them
hidden  joins only the build loop  -> collides, never painted
phantom joins neither              -> painted, holds nothing
No new node types. No collision check removed.

beats.label: The tower
beats.narration_text: The finish sits in a shaft above the floor. A test asserts a normal jump cannot reach it, so the mechanic is load-bearing. You get in by falling upward. Then Enter replays it clean.

beats.label: Verdict
beats.narration_text: So what is here. A platformer whose central mechanic is not a jump but a question - is what I am looking at real. Twenty-two landings past the original section. A finish the mechanic is required to reach. Seven distinct ways the world misleads you, every one of them with a learnable rule. Seventy mechanics checks and nine keyboard checks passing, including all twenty-five the starter shipped with, none weakened - and the movement tuning byte-identical to the original, which is the constraint the whole design had to fit inside. Two questions stay open by design: whether the Betrayal reads as fair or as cheap, and whether the environmental clues are legible at speed. Both are questions only a player can answer, and the playtest that produced this build already proved the point - it found three things every automated check had passed straight over.

artifactLines: WORKS  the mechanic IS the theme - checking what is real
WORKS  22 landings; finish unreachable without the feather
WORKS  7 kinds of lie: hidden, phantom, mirror, spikes, doors
WORKS  70 + 9 checks pass; tuning.gd byte-identical
OPEN   is the Betrayal fair, or cheap?
OPEN   are the environmental clues legible at speed?
LIMIT  3 rows of the human playtest still unverified

qc.sparse_reason: The verdict is six short lines that separate what works from what is unsettled. They are read aloud and meant to be read along with; padding the safe area with decoration would compete with the only thing on the card that matters.

beats.label: Where this goes
beats.narration_text: And it is one chapter of five. The design document carries four more, each inverting something different. The Forest Below, where the world stays upside down and objects exist only while you are not looking at them. The City That Doesn't Exist, where districts render differently depending on which way you approach. The Memory, where you start finding your own handwriting in a place you have never been. And The Other Side, where the inversion turns out not to have been an accident at all. Those are designed, not built, and this film will not pretend otherwise. The next concrete step is smaller and already specified - a room where the environmental clues contradict each other, and the player has to work out which to trust. The rule is designed: heavy things fall where gravity puts them and cannot lie. Paper and dust can be blown anywhere.

artifactLines: TWO    The Forest Below - objects exist while unobserved
THREE  The City That Doesn't Exist - perception inverts
FOUR   The Memory - you recognise a place you never visited
FIVE   The Other Side - the inversion was deliberate
NEXT   a room where the clues contradict each other, and
heavy objects are the ones that cannot lie

qc.sparse_reason: A reference card read aloud. Seven short lines the viewer is meant to read along with; decoration would compete with them.

beats.label: Who did what
beats.narration_text: Credit where it is owed. Narasimha Reddy Valam set the direction and made every design call that matters here - rejecting a costume-swap character for one built out of the mechanic, rejecting five thin levels for one chapter done properly, insisting the world teach through objects rather than instructions, and looking at an early build that passed every test to say it had no idea in it. That note is what produced the game you have just watched. Claude Code wrote the implementation, the tests, the capture harness and this narration - and got things wrong on the way, which are logged rather than hidden. The revision demonstrated throughout is commit c898a4b.

artifactLines: NARASIMHA REDDY VALAM - direction and every design call
rejected the costume-swap character
rejected five thin levels for one honest chapter
called the first build out as having no idea in it
CLAUDE CODE - implementation, tests, capture, narration
got the charge economy wrong; 3 tries at the debris
twice misdiagnosed a capture bug before measuring it

qc.sparse_reason: A credits card. The split between human and AI work is the content; padding the frame would make it harder to read, not easier.

beats.label: Your turn
beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it is a cheap experiment with a large payoff. Open your own starter and find the two places it walks its level data - the loop that builds colliders, and the loop that draws. Add one array that joins only the first. You will have a floor a player can stand on and cannot see, in about twenty lines, with every existing test still passing. Then go and find out whether your players read it as clever or as a trick. That answer is not in the code.
